Maladaptive Strategies.value: I remind myself it could have been worse

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't deal with even the slightest upset
I can't stop bad things from happening to me
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: 'Listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home' implies a home-intrusion/assault threat script. For a terrorism trauma in a combat pilot, this is not impossible, but it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile because no other items indicate a home-invasion-type trauma context.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typically linked to sexual assault or interpersonal violation. In this profile it does not fit well with terrorism trauma and is not supported by the other selected triggers, threat, or strategy items.

issues.item: Male Presence: Being alone with men
issues.explanation: 'Being alone with men' as a trigger suggests an interpersonal male-perpetrator association. That conflicts with the stated terrorism trauma unless there was an additional gendered assault component, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
The event that shattered Elena’s life occurred on a clear morning in Kandahar, during what should have been a routine pre-flight check. As she crossed the tarmac toward her F-16, a deafening blast from a concealed IED threw her sideways into the fuselage. The next few minutes were a blur of ringing ears, acrid smoke, and the sight of her crew chief’s blood soaking through his flight suit. She dragged him to cover, but the image of his face—and the noise—never left her. Now, five years later, Elena is a 45-year-old single woman still flying combat missions, but the cockpit has become a cage.

The most immediate triggers are physical. When Elena feels ill—a headache, a queasy stomach—she is flooded with the visceral memory of that morning, the nausea of shock and the taste of jet fuel. This feeling of being unwell instantly reinforces her belief that she cannot cope with even the slightest upset. She has come to believe that any bodily discomfort signals impending collapse, that the world is a dangerous place and she is helpless to stop bad things from happening. A simple cold can spiral into hours of catastrophic thinking: *I can’t deal with this. It’s only a matter of time before something worse happens.*

Crowded places are another potent trigger. Walking through the base exchange or a busy market, Elena’s chest tightens as the press of bodies replicates the crush of personnel after the blast. She scans every face, certain that someone is following her, and checks behind her constantly. These environments make her feel the world is inherently threatening, and she has come to believe she can’t stop bad things from happening—that she is a target. To manage this, she avoids enclosed or confined spaces entirely, taking stairs instead of elevators and sitting near exits. She also smokes more, lighting one cigarette after another as a way to steady her hands and quiet the hypervigilance. The smoking, however, keeps her alert and on guard, which in turn makes her more sensitive to loud noises—the crack of a backfiring truck or a slammed door—and these sounds then send her back into the loop of feeling ill and crowded by memory.

Her hypervigilance is constant. Elena sleeps poorly, waking at every creak of her apartment, and during the day she is superalert, cataloging threats. This watchfulness feeds directly into her negative appraisals: the more she scans for danger, the more evidence she finds that the world is dangerous and she cannot cope. She tells herself that at least it could have been worse—a downward comparison that offers brief relief but never lasts. The threat monitoring also amplifies her triggers: being on guard makes her more likely to notice the press of a crowd or the onset of nausea, and these sensations then confirm her helplessness. After a particularly bad week, she found herself looking behind her so often on the flight line that a fellow pilot asked if she was okay. She laughed it off, but inside she was certain she was falling apart.

The cycle has tightened over months. Her avoidance of enclosed spaces means she no longer attends squadron briefings in the small conference room, citing paperwork. The smoking, meant to calm her, keeps her wired and exacerbates her sleep problems. Each time she feels ill, she interprets it as proof that she cannot handle the next mission, which makes her more vigilant, which makes her more sensitive to triggers, which drives more avoidance. What finally brought Elena to seek help was a moment in the cockpit last week: a sudden stomach cramp during pre-flight, and she froze, unable to even reach for the checklist. She sat there for five minutes, heart pounding, convinced she was about to die. She is most afraid that this fear will ground her permanently, but she is also terrified of what might happen if she stops being watchful. She hopes, quietly, that someone can help her find a way to live without the constant scanning—without feeling that the next loud noise will be the last thing she hears.
